deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It continues a set of notes on ancient history, specifically the wars of the Diadochi (Alexander's successors). These look like lecture or reading notes and are not a mathematical manuscript. The previous page covers the battle of Gaza; this page narrates the following events:

- Seleucus returns to Babylon with a small force (1000 men, per the previous page). His army soon grows, and in 311 he takes Babylon.
- A peace is concluded (the Peace of 311 BC): each party keeps what it holds, and Seleucus is excluded.
- The terms of the peace: the Greek cities are to be free, and the young Alexander (Alexander IV) is to take the throne when he comes of age. The word 'König' was written and struck out before 'Alexander'. A marginal note says he was '11 Jahr alt' (11 years old).
- Cassander ignores this and, the page says, has Alexander and his mother (Roxane) executed in 311.
- Antigonus then sends Demetrius against Seleucus. Demetrius achieves little: he takes the city of Babylon but cannot capture the citadel. The next page continues: '...and had to withdraw.'

There are no formulas, computations or derivations to reconstruct. The only numbers are historical dates (311) and an age (11).
errors: Not mathematical; the only checkable content is historical dating.
Seleucus' recapture of Babylon is usually dated 312 BC, right after Gaza; the Seleucid era begins in autumn 312. The page gives 311.
The murder of Alexander IV and Roxane by Cassander is usually dated c. 310/309 BC, not 311.
Alexander IV was born in 323 BC, so at the Peace of 311 he was about 12, and about 13 or 14 at his death. The marginal '11 Jahr alt' is slightly low.
Demetrius' Babylonian campaign is usually dated 311/310 BC; the text's narrative order is otherwise standard.
